Listen to this article Share Victor Fingesi, national secretary of the Action Democratic Party (ADP), has called on the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) not to recognise a version of the party’s Constitution reportedly submitted by the suspended National Chairman, Yabagi Sani. In a statement in Abuja, Fingesi said Sani continues to issue official correspondence in the name of the party and make representations on matters that go to the foundation of its constitutional identity, notwithstanding his suspension. He said Sani reportedly wrote to the Chairman of INEC, Joash Amupitan, urging the Commission to recognise and accept a version of the ADP Constitution that is neither known to nor validly adopted by the party through the prescribed constitutional procedures. Fingesi described the action as an unacceptable attempt to undermine the supremacy of the party’s Constitution and substitute established institutional processes with unilateral decisions. He said that it was not an isolated incident, adding that over the past three years, Sani has repeatedly introduced purportedly revised versions of the ADP Constitution, effectively turning constitutional amendment into an annual exercise driven by personal discretion rather than established procedure. According to the statement, at the 2024 and 2025 National Executive Committee (NEC) meetings, Sani presented different versions of the Constitution for consideration and adoption, disregarding the clearly stipulated requirements governing constitutional amendments. Fingesi cited Article 55.1.1 of the ADP Constitution, which states: “No amendment of the Constitution shall be valid unless made after three years by a resolution passed by two-thirds majority of members present and with the consent in writing of the Ethics and Values Council and subsequently to vote at the National Convention.” He said Articles 55.1.2 and 55.1.3 prescribe additional requirements that must be satisfied before any proposed amendment can acquire constitutional validity. “These provisions are not decorative clauses. They are binding safeguards designed to protect the party from arbitrary alterations, preserve institutional continuity and ensure that no individual, irrespective of position can place himself above the Constitution,” Fingesi said. He said to the best of their knowledge, Sani has not demonstrated compliance with these mandatory requirements in respect of the versions he has sought to introduce. “It is therefore deeply concerning that he continues to make representations to INEC on the basis of such documents,” he said. Fingesi consequently urged INEC to subject the latest version submitted by Sani to appropriate scrutiny and decline to recognise any purported amendment that has not satisfied the constitutional and regulatory requirements. Party Logo: Another instance of unilateralism Fingesi said the same disregard for due process was evident in Sani’s handling of the party’s registered logo. He said at a NEC meeting in 2024, Sani unilaterally introduced a redesigned party logo without following the appropriate institutional procedures or securing the requisite approvals from the relevant organs of the party. He said the original and registered ADP logo is a square bearing a right hand holding an open book, a distinctive symbol representing knowledge, enlightenment and progress. In the redesigned version he introduced, he said, the hand, a defining element of the party’s identity, was removed while the square was changed to a circle. “Such a fundamental alteration to a political party’s registered identity cannot be treated as a matter of personal preference or administrative convenience,” Fingesi said. He said Part 9 of INEC’s Regulations and Guidelines for Political Parties 2026 sets out 13 conditions governing changes to the logo of a registered political party. He said these requirements exist to ensure transparency, institutional authorisation and regulatory compliance. “A party leader cannot simply redesign the party’s identity and expect the electoral regulator to legitimise the outcome without compliance with the prescribed procedures,” he said. He said the reported rejection of the proposed alterations by INEC further underscores the importance of respecting the regulatory framework. A dangerous pattern that must not continue Fingesi said the developments reveal a troubling pattern of disregard for institutional authority, constitutional limitations and the principle of collective decision-making. He said they also provide important context for understanding the controversies that characterised the party’s last National Convention, particularly the attempts to circumvent established processes surrounding the emergence of its presidential candidate, Ambassador Aliyu Bin Abbas. “The ADP cannot afford to become an institution where its Constitution is subject to the changing preferences of one individual, where party symbols can be altered without due process and where established democratic procedures are treated as optional,” he said. “No political party can credibly preach constitutional democracy to Nigerians while tolerating constitutional violations within its own ranks.” “The Constitution must remain supreme. Party institutions must be respected. Decisions must emerge through legitimate processes, not unilateral declarations.” A call to salvage ADP Fingesi called on all well-meaning members of the ADP across the National Working Committee (NWC), State Chapters and other recognised organs and structures of the party to rise above personal interests and join the effort to safeguard the integrity and future of the institution. “This is bigger than any individual, faction or political ambition,” he said. “It is about preserving the ADP as a credible democratic platform governed by rules, principles and respect for the rule of law.” “We must collectively resist every attempt to personalise the party, distort its constitutional identity or undermine the regulatory authority of INEC.” “The future of the ADP depends on our willingness to defend its Constitution today.” “The ADP belongs to its members, not to any individual. Its Constitution is binding on everyone without exception,” he said.
